#5819. The Ford Maverick Has Some Clever Hidden Features Most People Don't Know About

It feels like trucks get bigger and bigger every year. The differences between modern trucks and their predecessors are abundantly clear when you look at something like a Ford F-150 from the 1970s alongside a modern version: cabs are getting longer, beds are getting shorter, and footprints keep expanding. This is, in part, the result of George W. Bush-era revisions to the Corporate Average Fuel Economy (CAFE) standards, which linked each truck's fuel-economy target to its footprint, holding bigger trucks to lower mpg targets.

While some automakers have abandoned the compact and midsize truck segments, the ones still going strong are pretty impressive. In particular, the Ford Maverick is nearly the perfect truck, even with its un-trucklike unibody design. And if its excellent hybrid fuel efficiency, spiffy handling, user-friendly tech, and agreeable ride don't sell it for you, then maybe some of its hidden features will.

You see, the 2027 Ford Maverick isn't exactly a what-you-see-is-what-you-get truck. The Maverick comes with standard and optional features that don't announce themselves with much fanfare but are highly useful when you know where to look and how to take advantage of them. Knowing how to access and use extra storage, onboard power, and a plethora of customizable safety features will take your Maverick ownership to the next level.

Yes, most pickups are designed for hauling, so lots of storage is to be expected. That's what the whole bed is for, even if the average truck owner doesn't actually use it for truck stuff. The Maverick goes above and beyond, though, in offering flexible and functional options, plus plentiful hidden storage. This should partially make up for the fact that its 54.4-inch bed is about a foot shorter than the smallest bed on an F-150.

When futzing with storage options in the bed, you'll find that the Maverick uses Ford's Flexbed design. This includes a multi-position tailgate and fixed tie-down points, two of which — found on the gate — double as bottle openers for when you're having a tailgate party or need a crisp pre-drive Topo Chico. A cargo management system with bed rails and a small cubby recessed into the body of the truck is also available, with a removable tray to unlock more space. There's even a QR code in the bed that links to ideas for exploring bed storage techniques. You can also option in-bed LED box lighting to keep the area illuminated while you're working in low light. Additionally, the bed has a grooved design intended to make it easy to build and install your own storage solutions using 2x4s or 2x6s.

In the cab itself, you'll find storage under the rear bench. It's big enough for a small backpack, camera gear, work boots, or whatever tickles your fancy. Door storage gives enough room for decently sized water bottles, and there's additional storage space behind the 13.2-inch infotainment screen. Of course, you'll find storage in the center console armrest, too.

It's not exactly a secret that you can option even the base XL trim with Co-Pilot360, a suite of safety and driver-assistance features. However, using the system to its fullest potential takes a little massaging, and you'll likely want to customize the system to your preferences for the best possible experience. After all, aren't customizability and adaptability the true meaning of truck ownership?

Depending on the trim and options, a Maverick's version of Co-Pilot360 can include pre-collision assist with automatic emergency braking, a rearview camera, blind-spot monitoring with cross-traffic alert, lane-keep assist, automatic high-beam headlights, stop-and-go adaptive cruise control with lane centering, evasive steering assist, and post-collision braking. Co-Pilot360 technology also covers towing aids like Pro Trailer Hitch Assist. However, not every driver will want to have all of these features active all the time, and knowing how to turn certain features on or off piecemeal will lead to a better experience overall.

Many of the features can be manipulated through the infotainment touch screen, using the Settings and Features menus. You can turn auto high beams on or off with a couple of quick taps, for example, by hitting Settings, navigating to the Vehicle Settings button, scrolling down to Lighting, and hitting the Auto High Beam button. You can also customize your lane-keep assist functionality by turning it off completely, by allowing the tech to assist you in staying within the bounds of a lane, or by turning the assist off but keeping the warning on. This last option allows the truck to alert you when it senses you're drifting out of a lane, but the assist won't kick on to correct the movement. Play around with your Co-Pilot360 settings to find the configuration you're most comfortable with.

Perhaps one of the most useful features on the Maverick, and one that many drivers are likely not taking full advantage of, is its set of power outlets. Each Maverick comes with two 12-volt power points in the cab and two pre-wired 12-volt leads in the bed. In the cab, you'll likely use the USB ports to charge your phone, but not everyone makes use of the leads in the back. You can choose your own power tech to install back there, and it can be used to power small electronics and charge batteries when you're out on a job or while having a tailgate party.

But wait, there's more power where that came from. Starting with the XLT trim, this Ford also gets the option to add two 120-volt power outlets, just like those you'd find in your house. Whether you work in a trade that requires you to use tools or need power for an extended camping trip, these outlets are super useful. One outlet is located in the rear row of the cabin on the back of the center console, and the other is in the bed near the left flank. The two share a 400-watt inverter.

These outlets give you the option of keeping laptops charged while on long road trips, running small power tools for jobs without good access to electricity, or using the truck as a makeshift generator in emergencies. You'll need to power the truck on first and turn off any other functions that might take power. When the orange light on the outlet is on, you know you have power, and you're good to go. If you're a clean freak, you could even keep a handheld vacuum in your truck to keep things tidy.

The Ford Maverick benefits from a special customizability system known as the Ford Integrated Tether System (FITS), which is extremely handy but not always well advertised. Ford FITS lets owners design and 3D print custom storage solutions to fit their specific needs. In your Maverick, you'll find FITS slots in the under-seat storage area, as well as on the rear side of the center console. Ford sells its own accessories for these slots, but the automaker also publishes CAD files that help users create their own unique designs while ensuring FITS compatibility. Taking full advantage of this feature requires that you have a 3D printer, or can at least get access to one, but it offers a level of customizability that's hard to find in today's automotive industry.

The sky's the limit when it comes to designing FITS-compatible gear, as long as it fits within the designated area, of course. The obvious applications for the system are things like a rear cupholder or phone holster for the center console and a cargo divider for the under-seat storage, but users around the world have made and published designs for all sorts of uses, including, bizarrely, a chicken nugget holder with a special slot for sauce, though this was designed for older models of the Maverick. There are tons of free designs available online, and all it takes is a quick web search to find just what you're looking for.

If you're brave enough to design your own gear, Ford also offers guidelines for success. The company recommends adding breakaway features to avoid damaging the console and suggests a maximum breakaway threshold of 17 pounds. At the very least, FITS is fun to experiment with to make your Maverick experience truly personal.

#5817. America’s New Shipbuilding Orders Are Expensive Bets on Fossil Freight

South Korea’s Hanwha Group owns the Philadelphia shipyard that has become a centerpiece of Washington’s attempt to rebuild American commercial shipbuilding. Its Hanwha Ocean and Hanwha Systems subsidiaries acquired the US yard in December 2024. The investment creates and sustains American production capacity and jobs while transferring shipbuilding expertise, technology and training from South Korea to US workers. The facility is in America, but its corporate ownership remains South Korean. The company’s published orderbook, however, tells a more complicated story: two liquefied natural gas carriers, four firm orders for oil and chemical tankers, and options for another six tankers. Three LNG-fueled container ships ordered by Matson in 2022 predate the current administration. The newer LNG and tanker orders come from Hanwha’s own shipping affiliates. They can help restart production, but buying ships from another company in the same group does not demonstrate that independent shipowners will pay US construction prices.

The price gap is difficult to dismiss. Kinder Morgan’s January 2026 investor presentation estimates that a new medium-range Jones Act tanker would cost more than $240 million and require a long-term charter above $115,000 per day to justify construction. The existing charter market was around $90,000 per day. Kinder Morgan operates 16 tankers, with its fleet fully utilized, yet the gap between current charter revenue and the cost of a replacement vessel remains substantial. High utilization establishes a need for shipping services; it does not establish a financeable order for a new American-built tanker at today’s prices.

Coastal petroleum shipping also competes with other domestic infrastructure. A 2025 report to the Commodity Futures Trading Commission estimated moving gasoline from Houston to New York Harbor at under 8 cents per gallon by pipeline, about 20 cents by ship, and roughly 35 cents by rail. These illustrative route costs do not cover every destination, and tankers remain essential where pipelines are unavailable. They do show why expensive new tankers cannot count on charter customers accepting whatever price domestic construction requires. Longer term, the International Energy Agency estimates that electric vehicles displaced 1.7 million barrels of oil per day worldwide in 2025 and could displace about 5 million by 2030 under its policy scenarios. That does not mean US tanker demand vanishes, but fleet investment must account for changes in the cargo market over several decades.

LNG export carriers have a more plausible near-term growth market, although their prospects are different from the prospects of LNG-fueled container ships. US gas exports may expand, and LNG tankers will be needed to carry them. The commercial test for a US-built LNG carrier is whether it can win an arm’s-length contract against established Korean, Japanese and Chinese shipyards. Hanwha’s plan to train Philadelphia workers through its Korean shipyards can strengthen US industrial capability, and affiliated orders can provide an initial production run. The central uncertainty is whether independent buyers will still choose these ships once the group’s internal demand and any cargo preference are removed.

A broader domestic vessel market already exists. US-flag Great Lakes freighters carried 71.3 million tons in 2025, much of it iron ore, limestone, cement, coal and other bulk materials. Those cargo flows will change as steelmaking and energy systems evolve, while ferry services, harbour vessels, inland cargo craft and multipurpose ships will still require renewal. Battery-electric and hybrid-electric propulsion offer practical options on routes with manageable energy requirements and reliable charging access. Large, long-distance bulk ships need a more selective technology assessment, rather than an assumption that every vessel can run on batteries.

Recent projects demonstrate what a committed customer can contribute to ship economics. CMA CGM, Nike and Gemadept launched an electric inland barge in Vietnam for a 180-kilometre round trip. Nike agreed to fill 90% of its capacity for eight years, helping justify a vessel reportedly costing about twice as much as its diesel equivalent. A dedicated charging installation and renewable electricity form part of the service. That is a commercially structured freight proposition, with its higher capital cost supported by contracted utilization and expected operating savings.

Electric propulsion does not cure the American shipbuilding cost problem by itself. Washington State’s three new hybrid-electric ferries carry a $714.5 million shipbuilding contract, and the state’s estimate including additional equipment and other program expenses is approximately $1.15 billion. Construction has started; the ferries are not yet in service. The path to a productive shipbuilding industry still runs through standardized designs, modular fabrication, trained workers, repeat orders, reliable delivery and falling labor-hours per vessel. It would be a mistake to treat electrification as a substitute for manufacturing reform.

Hanwha’s South Korean capital and know-how could contribute to that reform by developing US suppliers and production skills that serve several vessel classes. That is a meaningful way to rebuild domestic capability even though the parent company remains foreign-owned. Its progress should ultimately be measured by independent repeat customers, improving construction costs and commercially competitive vessels, rather than affiliated orders or investment announcements. A US maritime strategy anchored to the fossil-fuel cargoes of today risks missing a growing opportunity to build modern domestic vessels for the freight, port and ferry services of tomorrow.

My TFIE Strategy Briefing assessment examines Hanwha’s orders, Kinder Morgan’s tanker economics and the market for repeatable electric and hybrid maritime construction. It follows my earlier analysis of the Jones Act’s shipbuilding capacity gap.

#5815. Rivian Doesn't Have Dealerships, So How Do You Test Drive One?

Running a business isn't easy. Aside from keeping on top of nagging accountants and office politics, you need to think about profitability and even sustainability these days – the latter two are particularly important if you're an automaker. The pivot toward electrification hasn't just been an opportunity for brands to re-establish themselves, but also for them to rethink how they run their business. Rivian is an excellent example.

The California-based marque is now well established thanks to vehicles like the R1S and the R2, which is even better than you'd hoped, and it's done so without having a single physical dealership around. Instead, it has various Spaces across the United States in places like Chicago, Denver, and New York. Interested customers can visit one of these Spaces to get a feel for Rivian's products in person before they order one through an online-only process. If you're looking to test-drive a Rivian before committing, this can also be done at many of the Spaces and Service + Demo Centers.

First, there are a few boxes you need to check before you can drive a Rivian. You'll need to be at least 21 years of age and hold a valid driver's license. Depending on the length and specific purpose of the drive, you might also need to bring proof of vehicle insurance. If applicable, you'll also need to bring and install your own car seat for any passengers younger than eight. Finally, you'll have to sign a liability waiver on-site before driving.

Okay, got all that checked? Good. Now you're ready to book the time and place of your test drive using the Rivian website. Your first decision is to pick which model you want to drive, and that includes the R1S – one of only two large SUVs with a 2026 IIHS Top Safety Pick+ award. Then you'll need to pick which location you'll visit and when, before submitting your key details (contact information, preferred popcorn flavor, you know the drill).

When you arrive at the Space — and we have no doubt you'll be punctual and fittingly dressed — you'll need to check in with one of the Rivian specialists. Expect a quick walkaround of your requested test car model after that, to get you up to speed on the car's features and key information. They probably won't tell you how many liters of popcorn the trunk can hold, though, so that may be worth asking.

With all the formalities taken care of, a Rivian specialist will accompany you on your test drive, which is said to typically last around 30 minutes and take place on public roads. If you thought it was going to be an off-road thrash to prove you have what it takes to race in the Dakar, sorry to burst your bubble. At certain locations, Rivian offers an extended demo drive for up to 24 hours. And no, that's not a ticket to race at Le Mans either.

Once your drive is wrapped up, you'll probably be asked the all-important question before being on your way. It's as simple as that.

#5814. Smarter Cooling, Stronger Reliability: Advancing Wind Turbine Gearbox Performance

As the wind energy industry matures, operators and service providers are increasingly focused on maximizing turbine availability while controlling long-term maintenance costs. Although major drivetrain components often receive the spotlight, one overlooked system can have an outsized impact on turbine reliability and performance: gearbox oil cooling.

Heat exchangers play a critical role in maintaining proper oil temperature and viscosity within wind turbine gearboxes. When cooling systems become clogged with airborne debris, dust, or organic material, oil temperatures rise, lubrication performance declines, and component stress increases. Over time, these conditions can contribute to reduced gearbox efficiency, elevated maintenance demands, and avoidable downtime.

“Wind operators today are balancing increasing performance expectations with the realities of aging fleets and rising maintenance costs. Technologies that improve cooling efficiency and reduce service exposure can have a meaningful impact on long-term turbine reliability and operational profitability,” according to Mike Erickson, HYDAC’s Market Manager for the Wind Industry.

Traditional “panel cut” heat exchanger designs have long been susceptible to clogging due to their tightly packed fin structures. In many wind environments — particularly agricultural, dusty, or high-pollen regions — debris accumulation can severely restrict airflow. Oil leaks can further compound the issue by trapping contaminants within the exchanger core, making cleaning more difficult and labor intensive.

This operational challenge has driven the need for more resilient cooling technologies designed specifically for real-world wind farm conditions.

HYDAC’s new “Square Wave” heat exchanger design represents a significant advancement in addressing these reliability concerns. Engineered to allow debris to pass more freely through the exchanger fins, the design minimizes clogging while improving cooling efficiency under demanding operating conditions.

The importance of effective cooling cannot be overstated. Wind turbine gearbox oil typically operates within an optimal temperature range of approximately 45°C to 65°C. Even modest temperature increases can significantly impact oil viscosity. According to field data, a 12°C rise in oil temperature can reduce viscosity by nearly 28 percent — affecting lubrication quality and accelerating wear on critical drivetrain components.

Field trials have demonstrated measurable operational benefits from the Square Wave design. During a one-year trial on GE 1.x turbines, the upgraded exchanger consistently reduced clogging and lowered maintenance requirements compared to traditional panel cut cores. Operators reported reduced up-tower cleaning time and fewer temperature-related cooling faults.

Field validation across multiple turbine platforms has further reinforced the operational advantages of the Square Wave design. In one case study involving legacy 1 MW-class turbines operating in the Pacific Northwest, a major renewable energy operator installed pilot sets of Square Wave heat exchangers as part of a cooling performance evaluation. Installation teams reported the upgraded exchangers integrated seamlessly into the existing platform with no retrofit complications.

After initial operating data demonstrated improved cooling consistency, the operator expanded the evaluation program with additional units. Long-term SCADA analysis later showed turbines equipped with Square Wave technology operate approximately 20 to 25 percent cooler than comparable turbines using conventional heat exchanger designs under similar operating conditions. The data also highlighted another important advantage: the Square Wave cores continued to maintain airflow and cooling efficiency in debris-heavy environments where traditional exchanger designs became increasingly restricted over time.

The successful deployment also generated interest from additional wind service organizations seeking retrofit-ready cooling upgrades that could improve turbine reliability while reducing maintenance burdens across aging fleets.

“What operators are increasingly recognizing is that small improvements in thermal management can create meaningful gains in turbine reliability, maintenance efficiency, and long-term asset performance,” said Erickson. “The field data we’re seeing continues to validate the value of designing cooling systems specifically for real-world wind operating environments.”

More recently, long-term SCADA data from Mitsubishi platforms further validated the technology’s performance. After two years of operation, turbines equipped with Square Wave heat exchangers operated approximately 19 to 25 percent cooler than reference turbines using standard exchanger designs under comparable operating conditions.

For wind asset owners and service providers, the implications are substantial: Improved thermal management supports healthier oil viscosity, more stable gearbox operation, and potentially longer component life. At the same time, reduced cleaning frequency and fewer cooling-related service events translate directly into lower operational expenditures and increased turbine availability.

As the industry continues to prioritize lifecycle optimization and energy production efficiency, innovative subsystem upgrades such as advanced heat exchanger technology are becoming increasingly valuable. Rather than waiting for costly failures or performance degradation, operators are seeking practical retrofit solutions that improve reliability without requiring major system redesigns.

“Effective thermal management is critical to protecting gearbox health and maintaining oil performance over time. By addressing one of the most common causes of cooling degradation — debris accumulation — operators can improve uptime while reducing unnecessary maintenance interventions,” said HYDAC’s Erickson.

For wind stakeholders evaluating ways to improve gearbox reliability, reduce maintenance exposure, and enhance turbine performance, cooling system optimization deserves greater attention. Proven retrofit technologies like advanced heat exchanger designs can offer a practical path toward improved uptime and operational efficiency without requiring major system overhauls.

As fleets age and performance expectations continue to rise, collaboration between operators, service providers, and technology partners will be essential to building more resilient wind assets for the future. Now is the time to evaluate whether existing cooling systems are supporting — or limiting — long-term turbine reliability goals.

“HYDAC’s goal is to help wind owners and service providers solve practical operational challenges in ways that create long-term value across the entire asset lifecycle. Innovations like the Square Wave heat exchanger are designed to improve reliability, simplify maintenance, and support greater energy production over time.”

Don’t let cooling system limitations impact turbine performance.

Proactive cooling optimization can help operators reduce maintenance exposure, protect critical drivetrain components, and maximize energy production across the asset lifecycle. #5813. Buc-Ee's CEO Said He Didn't Want To Operate In Blue States, And Now There's Stores In At Least Five More

I had the pleasure of experiencing Buc-ee's Beaver Nuggets for the first time on a recent road trip. It's an experience I'll get to repeat soon as the popular chain of ginormous gas stations and convenience stores expands into my adopted home state of Arkansas, among other places. It'll be interesting to see if the midterm election results affect those expansion plans, as Buc-ee's president and co-founder Arch "Beaver" Aplin III has expressed a desire to avoid blue states, according to Fox Business.

At the grand opening of a new location in Benton, Arkansas, Aplin said:

"I'm starting to realize life's too short to try to build in places that people don't appreciate what you're bringing, versus a place like this where people do appreciate what you are building," he said.

Conservative states typically promote business-friendly and family-oriented policies that align with Buc-ee's values, Aplin said.

"That leadership, that concept, that idea of conservative, business-friendly, family-oriented concept works so much better if it trickles down from the very leadership from the top at the governor's office, at the congressman, at senator, at the mayor, the representatives," he said.

The thing is, Aplin no longer has that choice. The blue tsunami of the midterm election has turned several states formerly controlled by Republicans over to the Democrats at many of those levels, and in some cases all of them.

Guess my election-interfering space lasers didn’t work this time 🤷‍♂️

The most notable upset from the election is right in Buc-ee's home state of Texas. President Trump hand-picked the scandal-ridden Ken Paxton to run against Democratic contender James Talarico for U.S. Senate, pushing out incumbent Republican John Cornyn during the primaries (maybe he won't be able to steal the Space Shuttle after all). Elon Musk invested more than $200 million backing Paxton's election campaign. Despite all that, Talarico won, making him the first Democratic Senator from Texas since 1993. Ted Cruz remains in the Senate, but possibly only because he wasn't up for re-election this year.

It's not just the Senate, either. Governor Greg Abbott lost re-election to Democrat Gina Hinojosa, and the Texas House gained a slight Democratic majority as well. Buc-ee's now finds itself deeply entrenched and headquartered in a blue state, as unlikely as it was for Texas to flip like this. If Buc-ee's really doesn't want to do business in blue states, it's going to have to find a new home. So will Elon Musk, for that matter, just five years after fleeing California for the same reason.

Where else could Buc-ee's move? Some states remain solidly Republican, such as Alabama, Florida, Kentucky, and Tennessee, and would likely welcome Buc-ee's "business-friendly and family-oriented values." Missouri remained red, though Democrat Fred Wellman flipped a House seat held by incumbent Ann Wagner.

In Arkansas, where Aplin made his comments back in August, Senator Tom Cotton, who encourages using your car as a weapon, remains in office. Opponent Hallie Shoffner ran a strong race based on the issues farmers are facing rather than the Trump Administration's culture wars. Even in crimson red Arkansas, every single county shifted more toward Democrats than in the 2024 presidential election, according to the Associated Press.

Other states besides Texas flipped from Republican to Democrat as well. In Arizona, Democrats will hold the state house, senate, and governor for the first time in 60 years. The Colorado House flipped from a 50/50 split to seven of eight seats going to Democrats. In Ohio, Amy Acton beat DOGE conspirator Vivek Ramaswamy for governor despite (or perhaps because of) a last-minute attack campaign against Acton featuring her estranged mother. The state house flipped Democrat, and Sherrod Brown ousted incumbent Republican Senator Jon Husted.

Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms will be not only the first Black woman elected governor of Georgia, but of any U.S. state ever. Similarly, the Mississippi Senate race (at the time of writing) remains too close to call, because Scott Colom holds a 0.1% lead over Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith. If Colom wins, he'll be the first Democrat Senator for Mississippi in 40 years, and the state's first Black Senator since Hiram R. Revels, who became the country's first Black Senator ever in 1870.

We'll have to wait and see whether this big blue tsunami has any effects on Buc-ee's expansion plans, as well as plans in states where it currently exists. Our own Brad Brownell called it the sickness at the heart of America, yet even he can't stop himself from loving it. And while I wouldn't call myself a beaver believer, I may have to take a motorcycle ride over to Benton for some barbecue and more Beaver Nuggets.

#5812. As Jackery Inventory Sells Out, Are Portable Batteries Set To Take Off?

I recently wrote reviews of the new Jackery HomePower 1000 Plus v2 and Explorer 100D. A few days later, a connection with Jackery messaged me that their Black Friday/Cyber Monday products had largely sold out. Just three days after launching on November 1. This includes 1000, 2000, 3600 and 5000 portable power and solar generator models. Additional models have sold out since then or will likely sell out soon. The recently launched Explorer 100D is still available in limited quantities at Walmart and Costco.

While Jackery will still take orders for Black Friday/Cyber Monday sales, most models currently listed for purchase will be on a preorder basis. Customers should check estimated delivery dates. Some restocking is expected in late November, although broader inventory availability may not recover until early next year.

While much of America was recovering from Halloween and election victory parties, portable batteries were selling out. This wasn’t the result of limited supply, but rather a massive, unanticipated increase in demand.

Between October 19th  and 26th, Jackery retail sales increased 755% at Costco, 106% at Walmart, 297% at The Home Depot and 442% at Lowes. For added perspective, at Costco alone, sales increased from 2379 to 20,343 over that one week.

Jackery is looking into what’s behind the massive increase in demand. Clearly, there have been climate-related disasters over the past year, including hurricanes and wildfires. Jackery’s collaboration with the Red Cross helps illustrate the benefits of portable power in emergency response. However, that only partially explains the growth. A related potential explanation is the growing push for household preparedness.  There are reports of at least 17 countries encouraging people to keep three to seven days of food, water and other essentials. Winter storm season, grid strain and rising energy costs could be stoking fears of potential power outages. The US FORTRESS America initiative has also added an emphasis on resilience. Together, these signals may be pushing “preparedness” beyond food and water to include power.

Preparedness is gaining emphasis with power becoming an increasingly important part of being prepared. The fear of “what if” can be a powerful motivator. Having backup power can keep the air handlers working for people’s furnaces. People on well water can keep the pumps running. Backup power can keep refrigerators full of food from spoiling.

Overall, Jackery is the global leader in solar generator sales volume and was named the “World’s No.1 Solar Generator Brand” by Frost & Sullivan. With over 15 years of experience and extensive safety protocols, the brand is well established. For the purchase of a product that manages risks, having a trusted brand is clearly valuable.

Although there has not been a detailed study of the consumer motivations, preparedness is likely a major motivator. However, versatile portable power stations have additional benefits. I keep finding new ways to use the HomePower 1000 Plus V2. And new possible benefits keep opening up.

Beyond providing emergency power, I can take power with me. I can set up an office remotely. I can run and recharge tools away from an outlet. I can power a radiant heater for a few hours while sitting outdoors. I can power an air conditioner for hours or run a fan all day. I can make coffee and cook food. In many ways, the batteries can replace functions once covered not just by a generator, but also a campfire or grill.

While using the battery, I also became more aware of my electricity usage. Seeing how quickly different appliances deplete the battery makes me realize where my utility bill is really going. Some things use less electricity than I anticipated, and some use far more. That awareness helps me to reduce my overall consumption.

And the UPS function can also save delicate equipment, as well as any work on computers and other machinery during a power disruption. I personally would not run a large print on my 3D printer without the backup battery. Providing stable power can extend the lifespan of many expensive devices.

The ability to integrate solar panels provides an additional level of preparedness, allowing the battery to be recharged by the sun when grid power is not available. However, solar can also charge the battery for daily use. While this may not yet be able to feed into the grid without additional equipment, people can reasonably use solar power fed into the battery to replace grid power at the point of use. When the regulations are figured out, balcony solar could expand the possibilities. All this can reduce people’s energy costs.

The battery can provide power when they need it, rather than just when the sun is shining. And when connected to the grid with a time of use (TOU) plan, it can charge when electricity is inexpensive and provide power when it is expensive. The savings from this alone could pay for the battery and start saving people money on their utility bills. And the grid becomes more stable in the process.

If the current battery capacity is not enough, Jackery makes expandible batteries to add more capacity.

In addition, the portable, scalable batteries can form the foundation of a whole home system. With greater utility communication, the added capacity could open up new possibilities for users to benefit while they help stabilize the grid. And they still benefit from the backup power. In addition, after seeing the capabilities, some people may even be inspired to look into going off-grid.

Of course, Jackery is likely not the only company seeing a surge in sales. I hope consumer demand and adoption is rising across the board. With a low barrier to entry and the ability to provide a level of preparedness, sales of portable batteries are likely to continue to grow.

Jackery is actively focused on removing the barriers to entry. Then the benefits of battery backup and portable power can be realized by more people. As more people see the benefits of portable expandable batteries, more people will want them. As more battery capacity is deployed, more applications can become viable. That not only has the ability to make homes more resilient, but also to build a more resilient grid. With the ability to shift consumption through distributed storage, more renewable energy can be utilized.

People who may have bought originally for preparedness will start to realize the broader benefits of their purchase. When people benefit from something, they will tend to rationalize it. This typically works better to change perspectives than trying to start with a rational argument. When people feel the relief of having backup power available for “what if,” they can then expand upon that with greater feelings of independence. Once they personally benefit from the storage that enables greater renewable adoption, they may increase their support for renewable energy. By addressing fears of “what if,” people may open themselves to thinking about “what’s possible.”

Of course, this might just be a temporary sales blip. But it could also be the start of a rapid expansion in home battery use. That could open up a wide range of new possibilities.

#5811. New York program funds $13 million in energy storage advancement projects

New York State’s Power Generation and Storage Innovation program has awarded nearly $13 million to 15 projects to support product development and demonstration of scalable long duration and other advanced battery energy storage solutions.

“Investing in next-generation energy storage technologies is critical to building a flexible and resilient grid that can make the most of our diverse energy resources,” said Doreen M. Harris, NYSERDA president and CEO. “These projects will advance promising solutions that can deliver power when it is needed most, strengthen grid performance and help drive down costs as we build a more affordable and reliable energy system for New York consumers.”

NYSERDA’s Power Generation and Storage Innovation program awards projects that develop and demonstrate innovative long duration energy storage (LDES) and other under-utilized, alternatives to traditional lithium-ion technologies. The awarded technologies include new designs for scalable LDES solutions that are over 10 hours in duration at rated power and will address cost, performance, and integration challenges such as grid congestion, hosting capacity constraints and lithium-ion siting limitations.

Public Service Commission Chair Rory Christian said, “Storage is poised to play an increasingly critical role in supporting a reliable, cost-effective, flexible, and lower emissions system as more clean energy resources are integrated into the grid, as well as enhance the efficiency of the state’s existing resources. NYSERDA’s dedication of these funds originating from innovation and research funding overseen by the Commission positions New York’s consumers to yield the promising long-term benefits expected by more complex and scalable applications of these technologies.”

All contracts are awarded to companies located in New York, partnered with New York companies or for development and demonstrations in the state. Today’s announcement supports NYSERDA’s Innovation and Research (I&R) program, which invests over $96 million per year to attract world-class energy innovators, reduce risk for private investors and remove barriers to clean energy adoption in New York State, leveraging $15 in additional investment for every $1 spent. NYSERDA has partnered with over 900 companies that have helped make more than 300 products commercially available for consumers, businesses and utilities.

Power Generation and Storage Innovation funding for comes from the state’s Clean Energy Fund.

#5810. Are These 9 Concepts And Sporty Coupés Pre-Ford Mustang Pony Cars?

History books love romantic tales, like the one where Lee Iacocca, father of the Mustang, was responsible for giving birth to a whole new category of vehicles: pony cars. Sure, he was behind the creation of the most popular such vehicle, but the pony car concept was in the brewing stage years before the first-gen Mustang Mk1. While not strictly pony cars, these concepts and production sporty coupés already flirted with the concept of an enthusiast-grade compact car.

Of course, we don't mean to diminish Iacocca's genius. Yes, he didn't invent the wheel, but he definitely read the room better than his counterparts. In fact, some of the cars featured in this piece influenced him to create the special team of engineers that worked on the Mustang. From early Ford-based compact sports cars like the Budd XT-Bird Concept and Ford Falcon Futura Sport to rear-engine fun machines like the Chevrolet Corvair Monza Turbo, these pre-Mustang models warmed the public to the pony car idea.

Iacocca wasn't the first to toy with the idea of a compact sports car for the masses. Edward Gowan Budd, one of the early 20th century's most important engineers and entrepreneurs, already had dabbled with the idea of a 2+2 sports car for the masses. Better yet, he pitched a working prototype of the XT-Bird directly to Iacocca, likely planting the pony-car seed in his mind.

The proposed car was based on a 1961 Ford Falcon unibody and a modified body shell from a 1955 to 1957 Ford Thunderbird. This let Budd's company, Budd-American Motors, stretch the Thunderbird's 102-inch wheelbase by 7.5 inches, turning it from a two-seater into a 2+2. Yes, the rear seats were tight and mostly unusable, but the 2+2 configuration became a hallmark of pony cars, allowing buyers to take their friends and family on a joyride.

Speaking of which, the XT-Bird Concept was equipped with a 170-cubic-inch (2.8-liter) inline-6 engine. Yes, it's not a V8, but Budd boosted it with a supercharger, so it should've been potent enough for the time. Power figures were never disclosed, but we know the XT-Bird Concept had a three-speed manual.

While the XT-Bird Concept influenced Ford in developing the Mustang, its clumsy attempt to modernize the classic Thunderbird fell flat. Budd smoothed out the Thunderbird's rear fins and accentuated headlight housings, resulting in a bland, somewhat forgettable design.

Ford never accepted Budd's XT-Bird proposal, but that didn't stop the ambitious engineer from making another attempt at an early pony car. Unveiled mere months later, the XR-400 Concept was another fully functional, production-ready sporty convertible.

This time, though, Budd used a Rambler Ambassador chassis and proposed the idea to American Motors Corporation. He went so far to create a full development plan, estimating a low $4.1 million to bring the car to market. Because the XR-400 Concept utilized an existing AMC platform, tooling and production would've also been cheaper than building the car from the ground up. Had AMC greenlit the XR-400, it would've beaten both the Barracuda and the Mustang to showroom floors, completely rewriting pony car history. Heck, it might even have saved AMC from the Chrysler buyout. Instead, AMC surrendered its head start and played catch-up with the other old-school pony cars using the 1968 Javelin.

Was the XR-400 good enough to save AMC, though? Well, it certainly looked sportier than the XT-Bird Concept, while also bringing AMC's 327-cubic-inch (5.36-liter) V8 into the fray. Budd even mounted the engine lower in the chassis, just as you'd expect in a sports car; shortened Ambassador's floor pan by 14.3 inches; and moved the cabin back 16.24 inches to give the car sportier proportions. The XR-400 Concept still offered 2+2 seating, though with less space in the rear than a Ford Mustang. Still, the XR-400 Concept was a textbook pony car convertible, two full years before the press coined the term.

Budd wasn't alone in developing a compact sports car for the masses. Ford concurrently worked on a mid-engine Mustang concept that could've completely changed the nameplate's trajectory. With a sharp, wedge-like design, pop-up headlights, two-seat cabin layout, and a tight 90-inch wheelbase, the Mustang I Concept served as the antithesis of Ford's lineup at the time: the Falcon, Fairlane, Galaxie, and Thunderbird.

The Mustang I was one of those cool Ford concepts that never made it to production, but it spearheaded the development of America's most popular pony car. Crucially, it was a fully functioning sports car. Yes, it only had a 1.5-liter V4 engine making up to 100 hp (gross) in race trim, but it was also featherlight at only 1,544 pounds. This race-car-level lightness was achieved by using an advanced space-frame chassis and aluminum body panels. As a result, the Mustang I Concept reached 115 mph, an impressive figure for such a tiny motor. And, sure, the engine was only a half-V8, but at least it revved to relatively high 7,500 rpm.

Handling was a big reason why Ford toyed with a mid-engine layout for the Mustang. Unlike later pony cars, the Mustang I Concept felt stable and balanced in the corners. It stayed flat during cornering, too, perhaps thanks to the integrated roll bar that strengthened the chassis. Ford was so convinced of the concept's abilities that it organized a publicity stunt at the United States Grand Prix at what was then known as the Watkins Glen Raceway, in Watkins Glen, New York. With star F1 driver Dan Gurney behind the wheel, the Mustang I Concept lapped the circuit almost as fast as an F1 car of the day.

While the Mustang I Concept introduced the famous horse emblem, it was the Mustang II Concept that was the real preview of the production car. Featuring a classic pony car shape with a long hood, relatively short rear deck, chopped roofline, and tri-bar taillights, it looked similar to the Mustang Mk1. It was 5 inches longer than the production car, which gave it a somewhat sleeker look, but the Mustang blueprint is definitely there.

The similarities weren't only skin deep. Like the production car, the Mustang II Concept was also built over a Ford Falcon unibody chassis, and had the right power train — a 289-cubic-inch (4.7-liter) high-performance V8 with a four-speed manual transmission. Like the first Mustang concept, this was also a convertible, albeit with a removable fiberglass hard top. In classic pony car fashion, the Mustang II Concept offered 2+2 seating inside. Being a concept car, it also previewed some tech-forward features, like an electric trunk release.

Much like its mid-engine predecessor, the Mustang II Concept was dressed in stark white with blue center stripes, and was also shown at Watkins Glen. This time, though, Ford passed the opportunity to show its abilities on the track. Still, Ford made sure the audience could clearly hear the V8 rumble by filling the valve lifters with wax, which apparently gave the engine a race-car-like big-cam note.

The Corvair was Chevy's revolutionary compact car designed to compete with the Volkswagen Beetle, featuring a rear-mounted, air-cooled flat-6 engine, multiple body styles, and a spacious interior. It proved to be an ill-fated attempt, but it also gave us one of the most interesting 1960s sports cars — the Corvair Monza Spyder Turbo.

The car that introduced turbocharging to the masses was the Mustang's opposite, given the Mustang's front-mounted, water-cooled V8. But it forced Lee Iacocca into creating the "Fairlane Committee" — the secret group of executives and engineers that decided Ford needed an attractive sports car, despite leading compact-car sales with the Falcon. And it was the Corvair Monza Spyder Turbo that served as the committee's inspiration, at least in terms of character and market positioning.

Of course, the Corvair Monza Spyder Turbo wasn't a pony car, per se. You could even argue that it's closer to the Porsche 911 Turbo, which arrived 11 years later with a turbocharged, air-cooled flat-6 in the back. Still, it was an enthusiast car with four seats, same as every pony car. The 2.4-liter turbocharged flat-6 also produced a healthy 150 hp, enough for a 0-60 sprint in 10.3 seconds, though, unsurprisingly, it suffered from significant turbo lag. For 1965, Chevrolet introduced the upgraded Corvair Corsa, which packed a larger 2.7-liter engine with 180 hp and accelerated to 60 in 7.8 seconds.

The Corvair Monza Spyder Turbo was also equipped with some enthusiast-grade features, like a standard four-speed manual; instrument panel with multiple gauges, including a tachometer; and bucket seats.

Strip away the attractive body style, and the 1964½ Mustang is essentially a Ford Falcon Futura. Launched as a direct answer to the Corvair Monza, the Falcon Futura, particularly in the Sprint trim, gave customers a taste of what the future of Ford sports cars hold.

The Futura Sport/Sprint shared most mechanical parts with the Mustang, and was even equipped with Ford's 164-horsepower, 260-cubic-inch (4.3-liter) Challenger V8 and a four-speed manual transmission. Yes, that's a far cry from the most powerful editions of the Mustang, like the 306-horsepower GT350, but good enough to serve as a stopgap model before Futura's more popular brethren arrived on the scene. Since the Futura was relatively light at 3,011 pounds, the V8 also propelled it to 60 in a solid 9.5 seconds.

To show its intention of attracting enthusiast drivers, Ford gave the Falcon Futura Sprint heavy-duty suspension and equipped it with a tachometer, bucket seats, and sporty steering wheel. Buyers could get the V8 as an option with all other trims, too, but would miss out on these features.

Despite having all the pony car features, minus the sporty styling, the Falcon Futura remained a low-volume proposition. Ford sold 15,081 during the first year of production, of which 10,479 two-door hardtops and 4,602 convertibles. Ford kept the Futura Sprint in production through 1965, but with the Mustang already in full swing by then, sales dwindled quickly. In fact, Ford sold 11 Mustangs to every Falcon, despite the Mustang being more expensive.

Studebaker might not be the first automaker you'd associate with pony cars. Still, it created one of the ultimate pre-pony sleepers with the Lark Daytona. From its compact dimensions to the highly potent engine in its R1 and R2 models, the Lark Daytona had all the ingredients for being called a pony car.

Based on the compact Lark, the sporty coupé Daytona version had pillarless doors and an unusual upright design. In that sense, it didn't look much like the "official" pony cars, but under its unassuming design, it hid a 289-cubic-inch (4.7-liter) V8. The engine was available in naturally aspirated (R1) and supercharged form (R2).

With 240 horsepower on tap, the non-boosted motor was already powerful enough to usurp rivals like the Corvair Monza Spyder Turbo and Falcon Futura, sprinting to 60 in the 7-second range when paired with the optional four-speed manual. Meanwhile, the supercharged version produced 289 hp, enough for a quicker 0-60 time of less than 7 seconds with the four-speed manual. The Lark Daytona was also available with automatic and manual three-speeds and a smaller 2.8-liter six-cylinder engine.

In many ways, the Lark Daytona punched way above its class, especially during the pre-pony-car era. Studebaker, though, couldn't outrun its misfortunes (our deep dive into Studebaker's rise and fall explains its desire for glory). The automaker was flying so high, in 1963 it launched a Corvette competitor called the Avanti. This sleek sports car was based on the Lark, but thanks to its more aerodynamic body, it reached a top speed of 178.5 mph using a 335-hp tune of Studebaker's supercharged V8.

The Valiant was crucial for Plymouth. It brought the brand back to life after dismal 1962 sales, and its sporty version, the Signet 200, served as the backbone for the world's first pony car, the 1964 Barracuda. Since the Valiant and Barracuda shared most of their mechanicals, it wouldn't be wrong to say the Signet was also a pre-Ford Mustang pony car. The blueprint was already there. The Valiant Signet 200 was a two-door hardtop coupé or convertible aimed at enthusiasts, equipped with front vinyl bucket seats, chrome accents, and from 1964 on, an optional 273-cubic-inch (4.5-liter) V8.

Initially, the V8 engine produced 180 hp, but for 1965, Plymouth increased the compression ratio and replaced the two-barrel BBD carburetor with a four-barrel one, boosting it to 235 hp. That engine could also be paired with an optional Hurst four-speed manual, though most models were equipped with three-speed manual/automatic transmissions.

The entry-level engine was a 170-cubic-inch (2.8 liter) Slant-Six, though, good for only 101 hp. Still, to showcase the car's sporty pretensions, Plymouth also offered a lighter all-aluminum 225-cubic-inch (3.7-liter) Slant-Six with 145 hp initially, but it was quickly replaced with a cast-iron version because of poor reliability. The Valiant Signet 200 was never available with disc brakes or heavy-duty suspension, upgrades that started being offered as options once the real pony cars took over.

Dodge also had a sort of an early pony car that shared the A-body platform with the Valiant. However, the Dart was noticeably less compact, stretching roughly 10 inches longer, which also increased its weight. Still, like its sibling, the Dart was available with the 225-cubic-inch Slant-Six and 273-cubic-inch V8 engines.

The Mustang might be the most influential, but the 1964 Plymouth Barracuda beat it to the punch by only 16 days, becoming the world's first pony car. Still, it wasn't a brand-new model, but a fastback body style of the Valiant Signet 200. See, the Barracuda didn't only share its platform and engines with Plymouth's compact car, but also carried Valiant badges on the body. Still, it was significantly more attractive, with a unique wraparound rear glass giving it a more dynamic, sporty look.

As far as performance goes, though, there was nothing to differentiate the two models. Like the Valiant Signet 200, the Barracuda was available with the 170-cubic-inch and 225-cubic-inch Slant-Six engines, alongside the 273-cubic-inch V8 with up to 235 hp in the Commando model. Enthusiast buyers could choose a Hurst four-speed manual with the V8, with Chrysler's three-speed auto also available.

Yes, the Valiant Signet 200 had exactly the same engine and transmission options, but from 1965, the Barracuda also had the supporting equipment of a true pony car. As part of the Formula S package, the Barracuda received an upgraded suspension and wider tires for sharper handling, with a tachometer inside.

These improvements let the Barracuda compete more closely with the Mustang, though Ford's legend was the better-rounded proposition. The Mustang was available with a more potent, 289-cubic-inch (4.7-liter) V8 with up to 271 hp, disc brakes, and a more comprehensive handling package with upgraded shocks, springs, and stabilizer bars.

#5809. Tesla & SpaceX Lost $420 Billion In Market Cap This Week — Didn’t Have To Be This Way

Many of you may remember that Tesla and SpaceX got significant boosts early on in their corporate lives from the Obama administration, the Democrat-controlled House, and the Democrat-controlled Senate. There’s a solid chance these companies would no longer exist today without that early support. Democrats in California and in the US government were also critical to consumer support for electric vehicles, air pollution standards for electric vehicles, and carbon credit markets that have led to billions of dollars of revenue for Tesla. Tesla would most certainly not have been able to rise and evolve as it did without all of that support — and, again, it’s questionable whether the company would have ever gotten profitable and been alive today if it didn’t have that strong support from Democrats. Republicans in power have not been willing to support EVs, put stronger pollution limits on gasmobiles, or require higher levels of fuel economy from automakers. Every time they have all the power of the US government, they go the other direction on these things.

Of course, we know that Elon Musk shifted to the right politically (to the far, far right) after a few things happened. Those key things were as follows:

Overall, historically, Democrats have been the ones who have pushed strong policies in support of the clean technologies Tesla develops and sells. However, because of the above (as well as a ton of seeming corruption and anti-democratic, oligarchic influence), Musk has been one of the top funders and campaigners for the Republican Party in recent elections. In this most recent midterm election, he was the single largest individual donor in the country, providing at least $447 million to try to get Republicans elected — completely unsuccessfully (well, like 99.99% unsuccessfully or something like that).

If Elon Musk had continued on his previous rather nonpartisan or bipartisan tendencies, who knows what this election would have meant for Tesla (and SpaceX). However, now that he has become the #1 Republican donor in the United States, and heavily stacked his social media platform in support of Republicans, one has to wonder how Democrats in control of Congress — and perhaps later on the presidency — will respond to the countless attacks Musk has waged against them. It’s logical to assume there will be repercussions. Perhaps they won’t target him unfairly, but they may well choose to investigate and seek punishments for illegal activity, provable corruption, and undemocratic behavior. Instead of this gigantic blue wave being something we could expect to help Tesla, everyone is now wondering if Tesla is going to face some serious consequences.

As a result, reportedly, Tesla and SpaceX lost $420 billion (yes, billion) in market cap following the election — ironically. Perhaps that value has changed now, but how fitting is it that this is the punishment the market is delivering for Elon Musk being so massively wrong politically. For now.

#5808. 5 Prestigious International Car Shows Where Automakers Reveal New Models

Changing industry dynamics and the rise of livestreaming have led many physical conventions and events to either go away entirely (most notably the Geneva Motor Show and the E3 video game expo) or shift to digital formats (Apple's major product keynotes). Thankfully, a lot of traditional car shows have stuck around globally and remain among the most important entries on the calendar for automakers.

Setting up a pavilion at an auto show, especially a reputable and longstanding one, can be expensive, but it gives automakers a global platform to unveil brand-new production cars, showcase wild concepts and designs, and introduce new technologies to journalists, industry executives, and prospective buyers. It's also always fun to walk through the pavilions at a motor show and check out new cars up close and in the flesh.

While hundreds of automotive exhibitions and trade shows are held across the world every year, there's an upper echelon of car shows for which automakers save their best reveals. These include long-running motor shows like IAA Mobility, exhibitions of growing significance like Auto China and Auto Shanghai, and Monterey Car Week, which isn't a convention but a week-long series of prestigious automotive events.

The Paris Motor Show, also known as Mondial de l'Auto, is one of the world's oldest automotive conventions, dating all the way back to 1898. Held biennially in the French capital, the Paris Motor Show has historically been a major platform for the country's top domestic automakers — Renault, Peugeot, Citroen, and the like — to reveal their latest and greatest to the world.

These include the Peugeot 402 in 1935 (one of the first European cars to feature a curvy, streamlined design), the Renault 4CV in 1946 and Citroen 2CV in 1948 (both instrumental in bringing personal mobility to a post-World War II, cash-strapped France), the Renault 5 Turbo in 1978 (a raucous 160-hp mid-engined supermini), and more. Landmark introductions from non-French automakers include the Lamborghini Sesto Elemento in 2010 and the Ferrari 250 Europa GT in 1954, along with the Porsche Carrera GT concept and Koenigsegg CC8S in 2000.

The 2026 iteration of the Paris Motor Show was held in October, and prominently featured concept cars like an all-electric revival of the Citroen 2CV, the striking Alfa Romeo Cuorerosso, the Peugeot E-T16 and RCZ Vision, the Alpine A310 Vision, the Renault E-Space, and the Fiat Multiplay.

Germany's International Motor Show or Internationale Automobil-Ausstellung, now branded IAA Mobility, beats the Paris Motor Show by just one year to claim the title of the oldest surviving car show in the world. Throughout its 129-year history, the biennial event has been held in various German cities, including Frankfurt am Main, Berlin, Leipzig, Cologne, and Munich. In a similar vein to the Paris Motor Show, IAA Mobility serves as a major showcase for Germany's big automakers, like BMW, Volkswagen, Mercedes-Benz, Audi, and Porsche.

Notable debuts at the IAA throughout history include the BMW 1500 in 1961 (it introduced the brand-saving Neue Klasse lineup), a concept version of the Volkswagen Golf GTI in 1975 (widely considered the forefather of hot hatchbacks), the Mercedes-Benz 190E 2.3-16 in 1983 (the record-breaking pioneer of sporty compact luxury sedans), the Audi RS6 Avant in 2007 (a super-cool V10-powered wagon), the Porsche 918 Spyder in 2013 (part of the holy trinity of hybrid hypercars), and many more.

The IAA Mobility held in 2025featured the motor-show debuts of the BMW iX3, the electric Mercedes-Benz GLC and Concept AMG GT XX, the Audi Concept C, the Porsche 911 Turbo S (992.2), and a near-production version of the all-electric Volkswagen ID. Polo supermini.

Held since 1954 and currently a biennial event, the Japan Mobility Show (formerly the Tokyo Motor Show) has cemented itself as a major venue for, you guessed it, Japanese automakers to showcase new cars, concepts, and experimental technologies. Toyota, Honda, Mazda, and Nissan particularly have been prominent participants at the Japan Mobility Show throughout its history.

The Japan Mobility Show has played host to the reveals of iconic cars like the Mazda Cosmo Sport in 1963 (the world's first mass-produced sports car to be powered by a two-rotor rotary engine), the Toyota 2000GT in 1965 (one of Japan's strongest rivals to European performance cars), the Nissan Skyline GT-R in 1968 (we're all familiar with this one, aren't we?), a concept version of the Toyota Prius in 1995 (the world's first mass-produced hybrid passenger car), and the Lexus LFA in 2009 (arguably the most sensational supercar from Japan).

At the 202 Japan Mobility Show we saw the reveal of the rakish-looking next-gen Toyota Corolla concept, along with other concept cars and prototypes like the Century Coupe, the Honda 0 Alpha, the wild six-wheeled Lexus LS luxury van, and more.

China holds not one, but two major global motor shows: Auto Shanghai and the Beijing International Automotive Exhibition (also known as Auto China or the Beijing Motor Show). These events are held in alternating years (Beijing in even-numbered years, Shanghai in odd-numbered years), which means there's a big car show in China on an annual basis. Since China is the world's largest automotive market by a huge margin, and a wellspring of innovation for new-energy vehicles (EVs and plug-in hybrids), Auto Shanghai and Beijing Motor Show are highly important platforms for Chinese and global automakers alike.

Chinese automakers like BYD, Dongfeng, and Hongqi have debuted some pretty wild stuff at Auto Shanghai and the Beijing Motor Show. Specifically, BYD showcased the Yangwang U8 (a full-size luxury off-roader that can perform a 360-degree tank turn and float on water for up to 30 minutes) and the Yangwang U9 (a 1,200-plus hp electric supercar that can jump short distances and drive on three wheels) in 2023. Hongqi debuted the Guoya limousine in 2025 as China's answer to established full-size European luxury sedans, while Dongfeng debuted the MHERO M-Hunter concept in 2024 — a bonkers-looking electric off-roader with a full carbon-fiber body and over 14,750 lb-ft of wheel-side torque.

As for the global carmakers that we're more familiar with, Mercedes-Benz pulled the covers off the electric G-Class at the Beijing Motor Show in 2024. At the same event, Lamborghini unveiled the Urus SE as the Italian marque's first hybrid SUV, and Mini revealed the Aceman as its first electric-only offering.

Unlike the conventional motor shows discussed above, California's Monterey Car Week is a series of automotive events centered on luxury, performance, and collector cars — both modern and old-school. Held across the Monterey Peninsula every August and tracing its roots to the first Pebble Beach Concours in 1950, Monterey Car Week is a must-attend event for any gearhead in the U.S., thanks to renowned and prestigious attractions like The Quail, A Motorsports Gathering; Exotics on Broadway; and the Pebble Beach Concours d'Elegance.

Automakers show up to Monterey Car Week to reveal exciting production cars, limited-run specials, and concepts. Bugatti has debuted one-offs and few-offs like the Destrier, Centodieci, and Brouillard during Monterey Car Week. American hypercar maker Hennessey showcased the Venom F5 Roadster in 2022 and the Blackbird in 2026, while McLaren also unveiled the McL 6GT concept this year to preview a forthcoming new model from the British brand.

In addition to exhibiting exotic machines, Monterey Car Week hosts auctions from houses like RM Sotheby's, and some of these are very high-profile — to the tune of tens of millions of dollars. The most expensive car sold at this year's Monterey Car Week was a 1964 Shelby Cobra Daytona Coupe, which went for the princely sum of $42.9 million. Also, a "Tailor Made" Ferrari Luce fetched a handsome $40 million, with the proceeds funneled entirely to charity. On the other end of the price spectrum, great cars often sell for under $10,000 every year at Monterey Car Week.

#5807. Alas, Poor Cybertruck, We Hardly Knew Thee

If you felt a ripple in the space-time continuum yesterday, yes, the rumors are true. All too sadly true. The Tesla Cybertruck EV, introduced to motorists in 2019 with great fanfare and a sales goal of up to 250,000 units per year, is slated to cross the rainbow bridge into the dustbine of automotive history sometime next year. Not to worry, Tesla fans. Rumor has it that Tesla’s Cybercab robotaxi will pick up where the Cybertruck left off — oh, wait. Hold, please…

Tesla is notoriously shy about releasing sales figures, but there are ways to reach an approximation. Earlier this year CleanTechnica calculated that the Cybertruck barely scraped by 2025 with just 17,012 units delivered. Even so, just one year earlier Tesla CEO Elon Musk was still pitching the 250,000 Cybertrucks-per-year goal.

Even though it is soon to be gone, the Cybertruck will never be forgotten. Much in the same way as the Edsel, “Cybertruck” will linger on as shorthand for a fabulously hyped product without an audience.

The Cybertruck was promised as a full sized, five-seat electric pickup truck with ample storage room. Tesla delivered on the zero emission angle, of course, and the five seats, too. However, the automaker failed to deliver on pickup truckyness in any substantive way (see entire CleanTechnica archive here).

So…don’t let the door hit you on the way out. Multiple electric pickup trucks are taking up the space left by the Cybertruck, including the forthcoming Ford Fathom alongside offerings from Rivian, Slate Auto, and other automakers.

Elon Musk himself announced the untimely death of the Cybertruck in a post on his social media site X earlier today.

“Tesla will be winding down production of the Cybertruck at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybercab production,” Musk stated somewhat blandly, perhaps expecting his audience to appreciate the good news about “increased Cybercab production.”

If so, Musk was probably disappointed to hear from X users like Ben McCombe, who skipped over the implication that the Cybercap would occupy more space in the Tesla Gigafactory in Austin, Texas. Instead, he zeroed in on the Cybertruck in a particularly pithy comment:

“Installed tooling to build 125k Cybertrucks a year.

“Made just $100m in gross profits from sales.

Tesla’s stock tanked on November 3 and the following two days, after Democratic candidates dominated the all-important mid-term elections in both Houses of Congress, and in statehouses across the country including Tesla’s home state, Texas. The power shift all but guarantees a more vigorous application of federal and state regulations governing Tesla’s products and operations.

Still, the automaker scored a partial recovery just a few days later. Tesla stock was swinging upwards as of mid-day on November 6, with Musk’s Cybercab announcement possibly factored into the partial recovery. However, those incoming lawmakers are going to be taking a close look at the Cybercab, and so far the picture is not pretty.

One sign of trouble emerged on September 3, when Musk failed to appear at a long-anticipated Cybercab launch event in Texas. The very next day, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration went out of its way to let everyone know that it is investigating Tesla’s self-certification for the Cybercab under the National Traffic and Motor Vehicle Safety Act.

“The US Department of Transportation’s National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) today announced that it has opened an Audit Query (AQ) to investigate Tesla’s certification that its new Cybercab meets all applicable Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards (FMVSS),” NHTSA announced on September 4.

NHTSA initially gave Tesla until September 30 to respond to a list of 21 questions about the Cybercab self-certification, then extended the deadline to October 30.

Anyone eager to learn how automakers go about self-certifying new models under the National Traffic and Motor Vehicle Safety Act will be sorely disappointed, unless they are privileged to read the documents Tesla finally submitted. “The tricky part is that in its public response, Tesla offered one whole sentence. ‘The entirety of this file is confidential business information,'” Carscoops reported earlier today.

So close and yet so far. While the Cybercab investigation is still bubbling away on the backburner, Tesla has also set itself up for a whole ‘nother round of investigations related to its newly unveiled “flying car,” part of a suite of high-end sports cars modeled after the original Tesla Roadster.

The Roadster reboot was slightly clouded by the release of a new documentary on Elon Musk’s rise to both automotive and political power, but just slightly. The automotive press went nuts over the spectacle of the new Tesla Roadster Rocket going airborne for a few seconds, then safely landing on all four tires with an assist from SpaceX-designed thrusters.

Whether or not that actually counts as a flight or just a thruster-enhanced jump, the Federal Aviation Administration has already stated that the Rocket does not meet its definition of an aircraft.

As of for the question of whether or not the vehicle can be used on public roads, that’s something for the NTHSA to weigh in on. On Tesla’s part, though, the automaker has reportedly stated that the Rocket is not designed for use on public roads. That seems to cut NTHSA out of the picture, though some industry observers have suggested that the agency could adopt a framework that encompasses vehicles with thrusters.

Musk himself has suggested that anyone who purchases the thruster-equipped Roadster can make it fly on a purpose-built tack on Tesla (or perhaps SpaceX) property, presumably in Texas.

The land use issue opens up a whole ‘nother can of worms regarding Musk’s operations in Texas. If anything, the offer of an off-road Rocket track seems could to let Tesla off the hook for the actions of any rambunctious Rocket driver who insists on trialing the car on public roads.

For the record, “Musk” the movie opened initially in Los Angeles and New York City on October 9. A wide release on hundreds of screens was scheduled for October 16, but the film’s distributor, Bleecker Street,” abruptly pulled back on the plan under new ownership. On October 27, representatives for the film contacted CleanTechnica to clarify that the “Musk” documentary was still showing on scores of screens around the country even after the dial-down. Either way, if you missed it in theaters, you can catch the whole thing — including the Cybertruck debacle and so much more — streaming as of today, November 6, on Amazon Prime Video, iTunes, and YouTube along with cable services.

#5806. Positive Antinuclear Antibody Test? This Tool Helps Show What That Means.

— Dramatically cuts time to definitive diagnosis of autoimmune disease in randomized trial

For patients ultimately determined to have an autoimmune disease following a positive antinuclear antibody (ANA) test, a digital aid made what is often a diagnostic odyssey more like a trip to the corner store, results of a randomized trial indicated.

Called AURA, use of the (relatively) simple tool cut the median time to autoimmune disease diagnosis by nearly 70% -- 43 days from the positive ANA test, versus 138 days with usual care, according to April Barnado, MD, MSCI, of Vanderbilt University in Nashville, Tennessee, and colleagues.

When applied to some 2,000 ANA-positive patients, most of whom were not ultimately diagnosed with an autoimmune disease, the tool had an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.79 (95% CI 0.73-0.86) for identifying those who did, the researchers reported in NEJM AI.

"By leveraging routinely collected, real-time EHR [electronic health record] data within a robust randomized pragmatic design, this study demonstrates a scalable framework for moving predictive analytics from theoretical validation into operational clinical implementation," Barnado and colleagues wrote. "Although future multicenter trials are required to establish external generalizability across diverse community practices, these findings illustrate that tightly integrated, interpretable structured-data models can meaningfully accelerate clinical care timelines for high-risk patients."

AURA stands for AUtoimmune Risk Assessment and combines a variety of demographic and clinical factors to produce a "risk score" for the likelihood that an ANA-positive patient has an autoimmune condition such as lupus or systemic sclerosis. ANAs are a hallmark of these diseases but very far from specific to it. One review from 2018 indicated that 2.5% of the general population has "significantly elevated" ANAs, with the authors writing that "[m]ost people with a positive ANA count are not diagnosed with autoimmune disease, and the probability of future disease is low."

Still, the presence of ANAs certainly raises the likelihood that autoimmunity is the reason. The clinical challenge is to identify those patients for whom it's worthwhile to pursue the additional rounds of testing and physical exams involved in a rheumatologic workup. Diagnostic odysseys are notoriously common for ANA-related diseases, with their highly variable clinical presentations -- Barnado's group noted that 7 years is the average time from symptom onset to diagnosis for systemic lupus.

In an earlier report, Barnado and colleagues described how they distilled data from about 2,000 ANA-positive individuals into a model that would pinpoint those most likely to have an autoimmune disease, via a numeric risk score. These data were of the kind routinely included in patients' EHRs: absolute ANA titer, numbers of billing codes for symptoms consistent with autoimmune disease, platelet count, and presence of a second autoantibody, along with age and sex. This initial training-and-validation model yielded an AUC of 0.83 for triaging patients into a rheumatologic evaluation.

For the current, prospective study, the researchers applied the model to a different set of ANA-positive patients seen at Vanderbilt, randomizing about 2,400 to either have their data analyzed with the model, with the resulting risk score conveyed to the treating clinicians via notification in Vanderbilt's EHR system or to usual care in which clinicians used only their own judgment.

Roughly 200 patients in each group were excluded after randomization, either because they were already scheduled for rheumatologic exams or because they had already seen a rheumatologist outside the Vanderbilt system. That left 954 assessed with AURA and 1,006 in usual care. Of the former, AURA identified 270 as high risk for autoimmune disease, making them eligible for an expedited rheumatology referral.

As expected, most patients in the final cohort were not ultimately diagnosed with an autoimmune disease: Within 800 days of the first positive ANA test, only about 8% of those evaluated with AURA ended up with such a diagnosis, versus roughly 5% of the usual-care group. This difference made sense, Barnado's group explained, because of the expedited rheumatologic exams available to those identified as high risk with AURA, who would thus be diagnosed sooner. One could also imagine that in the usual-care group, absence of an EHR flag to suggest a rheumatologic referral would mean that some high-risk patients would never get one.

Confining the analysis to those in the highest quartile of risk scores indicated that 20% were eventually diagnosed with an autoimmune disease, and nearly all of them got that diagnosis within 3 months of their first ANA-positive test. Notably, patients in the usual-care group were also scored with AURA but this was not relayed to clinicians; only about 12% of those with high scores received an autoimmune diagnosis, and it took considerably longer for those who did.

The researchers boasted that their tool's simplicity, both in the small number of variables employed and its regression-based statistical machinery, should make it more useful in the clinic than those powered by big AI models. "Unlike black-box deep-learning algorithms that can obscure decision-making," they wrote, "our model allows providers to easily verify the clinical factors driving the risk score."

An important limitation was the single-center data source, both for the model's development and its testing in the current study. Also, the authors acknowledged that it was impossible to distinguish "the independent predictive utility of the clinical prediction model from the effect of the early rheumatology referral invitation sent to providers" -- merely sending all ANA-positive patients for rheumatologic evaluation would likely speed up diagnosis, though costly and inefficient.
